hook: I can't afford a lawyer. Can I **argue my own case**?
hook_q: Can I argue my own case without a lawyer?

slides.title: Yes, you can **appear in person.**
slides.body: In a civil case, any appearance, application or act in court may be made by you in person, by your recognised agent, or by a pleader.
slides.note: court can ask you to come personally
slides.ref: Code of Civil Procedure 1908 · Order III Rule 1

slides.title: Only **advocates** practise law.
slides.body: Advocates are the only class of persons entitled to practise law. But a court may permit a person who is not an advocate to appear before it in a particular case.

slides.title: Accused? You have a **right to a lawyer.**
slides.body: Anyone accused of an offence before a criminal court may, as of right, be defended by an advocate of their choice.

slides.title: Can't pay? **State-paid advocate.**
slides.body: In a trial or appeal, if the accused has no advocate and the court finds they lack the means to hire one, the court must assign an advocate at the State's expense.

slides.title: Free legal services: **who qualifies.**
list: Members of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes
People below an income limit (depends on your State)

sources: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 – Order III Rule 1
caption:
Can't afford a lawyer? Here's what the law says about arguing your own case. 👇

1️⃣ In a civil case, you can appear and act in court in person
2️⃣ The court can still direct you to appear personally
3️⃣ Only advocates practise law, but a court may permit a non-advocate in a particular case
4️⃣ An accused person has the right to be defended by an advocate of their choice
5️⃣ If an accused can't afford one, the court must assign an advocate at the State's expense
6️⃣ Free legal services are available to women, children, SC/ST members, persons in custody and others

Source: CPC, 1908 (Order III Rule 1); Advocates Act, 1961 (Sec 29, 32, 33); BNSS, 2023 (Sec 340, 341); Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 (Sec 12)
